items.titleEn: Arteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own making | Barney Ronay
items.summaryEn: Refereeing is now an impossible job owing to the culture of micro-analysis the Arsenal manager has helped to createA gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. bodyEn: A gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. Nobody really knows who said this first. But it could easily be a line from the Elite Football Manager’s Guide to Press Conferences (Premier League edition). Because nothing happens by accident in these spaces.

Every word spoken in front of the board covered in adverts is metered and planned. A manager is never angry, or concerned, or even charming unintentionally. The game is the game, but so are all the other bits spilling out either side of it.

It was hard not to think about this while listening to Mikel Arteta talk about the penalty awarded to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light for a perceived act of grappling on Dan Ballard by Ezri Konsa. This is said with genuine professional respect. As everyone who has ever done a podcast knows – and this is, let’s be clear, everyone – there are lost Amazonian tribes discussing Girls season three in their own dark corner of Spotify – there are moments when you just have to flip the switch, up the energy and turn on full clip‑this‑bit‑up‑please‑Dave sincerity mode.

Arteta did this beautifully in the moment, appearing genuinely struck by what he was saying, radiating wounded integrity, like a disappointed junior headmaster appealing for the return of the school minibus keys.

Let’s be clear though. Arteta is not “very worried” about all this. He’s not “sad” or indeed, as he later emphasised for good measure, “really sad”. He’s not concerned solely with “protecting the game”, speaking here for all of us, just a fan of football.

Come off it. This is a manager we know to be obsessed with the most marginal of gains, to micro-plan the micro-details. As is all elite sport now. There has been talk of rowing coaches installing fibreglass toilet seats at their training hubs having calculated the average athlete spends 20 minutes in there and this is all key glute management time. Arteta loves this stuff. There’s no way Ben White isn’t sat fiddling with his phone at the training ground on a gold-standard Easy‑Cup Mega-Soft Evacu-Throne.

So it is with his public statements. This will have all been gamed and contingency‑planned in advance. And for hard, rational, tactical reasons, because this is how the game is played and run now. So what does it mean?

There are three things we know for sure. First, Arteta was right. This was a bad refereeing decision. Most obviously it was factually wrong. Ballard very skilfully pulled Konsa down on top of him, while simultaneously feigning shock that such a thing could happen.

It was doubly bad because the referee’s response was pre-planned, flagged by the early-season chat about refereeing in a more interventionist fashion. Go into any situation with a voice in your head, a vaguely worded mission to fulfil: this will skew your judgment.

The second thing is that referees are not biased. They’re just not very good. Two things have happened to them. First, the barrage of information to be absorbed in real time during a game is now utterly mind-boggling.

Most referees are not from a high-pressure data-processing background. These are not military pilots or traders on a currency floor. Less than a quarter have an academic degree. The task is beyond them. This is not a slur or an insult. It’s a simple description of what is happening, as supported by the evidence.

This is doubly annoying because referees have become fundamentally confused about their role. Referees are not ringmasters, or curators of the spectacle. They don’t get to decide what our sport should look like. Pro Ref is a private company with no locus standi to rule on the aesthetics of football. A referee should exist at the very edge of the spectacle. You’re not a local government planning officer with a mandate to decide which double-glazed French doors are or aren’t in character with the neighbourhood. Stop getting football not just wrong, but wrong.

But Arteta was also ready for this. Arsenal’s coaches will have known this would happen at some point. That press conference response was already in the chamber. Arteta may even have practised his sad-not-angry face, his key lines.

And this would be the correct thing to do. None of this is breaking the rules, just as Arsenal are not a dirty team or a bunch of cheats. They play the game that is being presented to us, a sport that is being made to operate at the edge of its own ludicrously micro‑analysed rules on small issues of physical contact.

Arteta’s Arsenal have been masterful at finding advantages in this. Defenders are very good at playing with the ball at their feet now. Defenders are not selected for their ability to resist physical challenges. It is logical to exploit this, just as it is logical to seek to protect your ability to do so by speaking in public about how the rules are applied. This is why Arteta is good, and why he wins.

It is also true that this has created a strange environment. The tone of the wider Arsenal fanbase is another element here. There is no one type of football fan. All human life is here. But the fact remains, the loudest voices in the online Arsenal hive mind, even the atmosphere in the stadium is unique in its absolute conviction of victimhood, of conspiracy, of a galvanising sense of adversity.

There is no other ground where every single refereeing decision, even the who-knows 50-50s, is so violently and eloquently disputed. There are supporters who seem to spend most of the game up on their feet in a state of performative, weaponised indignation, whose entire interaction with the spectacle is an attitude of aggrieved injustice.
This makes sense, too. It speaks directly to the game we have created. Aggrieved middle-aged rule pedantry. This is the new cauldron of hate.

Is it based in reality? Not perhaps on the outline numbers. Arsenal have been awarded more fouls than any other team this season. Only six teams last season had more fouls awarded against them, and the same the year before. They had the fewest yellow cards last season. They haven’t had a single red since they had six of them in 2024‑25.

Still, certain key incidents continue to grate and fester. There was the incorrectly denied penalty claim for Bruno Guimarães at Aston Villa. The balls-up with VAR lines against Brentford in 2023, which, if it really was deliberate conspiracy-cheating, was the worst, most public attempt at deliberate conspiracy-cheating ever conceived.

There is discontent at the way some rules seem to be applied more severely to Arsenal, the silly little stuff like delaying or fiddling about with restarts. But then again, if you make the game about that, if you plan to play on the margins, and successfully so, more stuff might happen in that place while you’re doing it.

Arteta has also played the role of arms-length rage conjurer expertly, has gone from rarely commenting on referees to heartfelt and carefully targeted critic. The Sunderland penalty award was a first opportunity to unload on the refereeing backlash to Arsenal’s tactics, to launch his pre-prepared defence; and to point out something demonstrably true. Referees have lost control of this, because the game has got beyond them.

In many ways this was a perfect storm for Arteta. Not just a decision that didn’t matter, because the penalty was saved. But a decision that was clearly incorrect too, a chance to get your lobbying in while very obviously in the right.

There will be more of this as the season plays out, as Arsenal work to preserve the advantages they have made for themselves in close quarters, tactical attack and defence. Factor in that masterful turn at a press conference j’accuse, and Saturday was a significant win in more ways than one.

items.titleEn: Lotte focused on how to become more clinical
items.summaryEn: Lotte Wubben-Moy says she and her teammates will be taking a moment to reflect on how to be more clinical in front of goal following Sunday’s 0-0 draw at home to Crystal Palace.
bodyEn: Lotte Wubben-Moy says she and her teammates will be taking a moment to reflect on how to be more clinical in front of goal following Sunday’s 0-0 draw at home to Crystal Palace.

Asked for her take on a game in which we produced so many chances but were unable to break the deadlock, Lotte said: “I think first and foremost, when you're unable to do the fans justice, who came out today and supported us from minute one to minute 90, that really hurts, not only on a psychological level but I think also pretty deep when it comes to how much we put out into the game today.
“A lot of us dug deep, but ultimately it amounts to nothing. We come away with losing points. That's not what we expect for doing it at our home here in the Emirates, so that's really tough to take.

“But I think looking at it pragmatically, we created the chances and ultimately just weren't able to put them away. That's something quite, I don't know, clear cut, you can change that easily. I believe in the strength of the team and the depth that we've got that we can push each other to come back and score more.”
We were relentless in our pursuit of that goal, but Palace continued to deny us defensively.

“I think credit to Palace,” Lotte agreed. “They put their bodies on the line. I think there were quite a few shots that came off the crossbar and just over. We can't say to ourselves, ‘oh, we didn't shoot enough’, because we did.
“Shots from the edge of the box, even creating one or two chances in the six-yard box, we had those chances too. I think it's a moment for us to reflect and look at how we can be much more clinical.”
Lotte added this she’ll want the place rocking for next weekend’s visit of Manchester United.

“Without a doubt, and I don't even think I need to say that because it just always happens. It's such a pleasure to play here in front of our fans. Yeah, they're just wonderful. I know all the new girls felt that energy today. I never take it for granted, so I feel that every week too.”
items.author: Stephen Wright

items.summaryEn: Renée Slegers and her team are under no illusions about their efforts in Sunday’s 0-0 draw at home to Crystal Palace.
bodyEn: Renée Slegers and her team are under no illusions about their efforts in Sunday’s 0-0 draw at home to Crystal Palace.
We pushed and pushed for the opening goal at Emirates Stadium, but were ultimately unable to make the breakthrough.

Reflecting on a frustrating draw in N5, our head coach said: “Disappointed of course, we were here to take three points. That’s what we were set to do, that’s what we expect from ourselves. We weren’t successful from that perspective, and that’s the most important, the result.

“Yes, there were really good things in our performance, some real positives. I think we had around 30 shots and plenty of box entries, but the ball didn’t go into the net, so we’re critical of ourselves.
“We will bring things that we did well today into next weekend. Of course, critical and disappointed of not getting the three points today.”
This match was as much about patience and perseverance as anything else, as we pummelled Palace with 30 shots, never slowing down our relentless pursuit of a goal.
But the Eagles stood firm to keep us at bay.
“Like I said, there’s a lot of good things in our football,” Renée said. “The variety of attacks that we set up, how we were intent and wanted to keep the tempo high in the game.

“From a mentality perspective, we kept going, we didn’t stop believing. So, there’s positives, but also very aware that we wanted and needed to get the three points today. Sorry for the supporters and we’ll do everything to be better next weekend.”
items.author: Stephen Wright

items.summaryEn: We were held to a goalless draw at home to Crystal Palace in the Women’s Super League on Sunday afternoon.
bodyEn: We were held to a goalless draw at home to Crystal Palace in the Women’s Super League on Sunday afternoon.
Our dominance throughout the game was met with stubborn defending from Palace to ensure the points were shared in N5.
APPLYING THE PRESSURE

Setting the tempo for a dominant first half, Georgia Stanway threaded the ball through to Alessia Russo early on, and she turned well before getting a shot away, stinging the palms of Pauline Peyraud-Magnin with a powerful left-footed effort.

Mariona Caldentey then lifted a half-volley onto the crossbar following a Chloe Kelly cross from the left, before Mariona slotted in Emily Fox, but Peyraud-Magnin rushed off her line to close the angle and make the save.
Leah Williamson won the ball from a Palace clearance in the 21st minute and was afforded time and space to have a go from distance, firing over the bar.

Continuing our hunt for the opener, Fox’s left-footed cross from the right was headed back across goal by Mariona and Russo was there to divert it towards goal, but Molly Bartrip was in the right place to clear the danger.

Just beyond the half-hour mark, Stanway did well to carry the ball into the 18-yard box before shooting just wide of the bottom left, and Kelly played a short corner to Kyra Cooney-Cross, her delivery hooked wide by Mariona.
The away side had their first sight of goal in the 35th minute, when Abbie Larkin’s free-kick was flicked on by Cooney-Cross and headed onto the roof of the net by former Gunner Teyah Goldie.

Back up the other end, Stanway teed up Ona Batlle on the edge of the area and she hit it just over the bar, before we flew forward on the counter-attack and Lisa Baum, who had switched from right to left, fizzed the ball across the face of goal, but Russo failed to hit the target.
ONE-WAY TRAFFIC
It was much the same story in the second half - our Gunners dominating with possession and chance creation but unable to break the deadlock.
Baum cut in from the right and smashed a strike towards the bottom right but Peyraud-Magnin was equal to it, before Batlle’s cross came out to Fox and her ball back in was touched wide by Russo.

Stanway then played a long ball forward to Mariona, who took it down well but curled just wide of the bottom right, and Russo found Baum on the right and she did well to sit Goldie down before shooting onto the bar and over.
With half an hour remaining, Olivia Smith and Stina Blackstenius came on as we looked to find the breakthrough, replacing Kelly and Cooney-Cross.
Moments later, Baum drifted in from the right again and went for goal on her left foot. Peyraud-Magnin spilled it before Batlle shot straight at the Palace goalkeeper.
We were denied again by Peraud-Magnin after Baum put Blackstenius through on goal, and Russo’s next effort was low but again the keeper made the save.
Stanway then tried her luck from distance, forcing Peyraud-Magnin to parry it past the post, but nothing came of the following corner.
Our next changes came in the 74th minute as Kim Little and Caitlin Foord replaced Mariona and Baum, before Frida Maanum came on for Russo in the 85th.
Smith struck wide of the bottom left from distance and Little shot over in the game's dying embers as we were forced to settle for a point apiece.
items.author: Stephen Wright

items.titleEn: Team news: Three changes for first WSL home game
items.summaryEn: Renée Slegers has made three changes to her starting XI for our first Women's Super League home game of the season.
bodyEn: Renée Slegers has made three changes to her starting XI for our first Women's Super League home game of the season.
We host Crystal Palace in a 2.45pm kick-off at Emirates Stadium.
Kyra Cooney-Cross, Chloe Kelly and Lotte Wubben-Moy all come into the line-up following last weekend's 1-0 win away to Brighton & Hove Albion.
They replace Kim Little, Olivia Smith, and Steph Catley, who will make her 100th WSL appearance if she comes on.

Summer signing Élisa de Almeida is on the bench for the first time, while Isabella Damm, Geraldine Reuteler, Selina Cerci and Taylor Hinds are not in the squad. Daphne van Domselaar, Katie Reid and Michelle Agyemang remain unavailable as they recover from injury.
LINE-UPS
Arsenal: Misa, Fox, Williamson, Wubben-Moy (C), Batlle, Cooney-Cross, Stanway, Mariona, Baum, Kelly, Russo
Substitutes: Borbe, De Almeida, Catley, Holmberg, Little, Smith, Maanum, Foord, Blackstenius
Crystal Palace: Peyraud-Magnin, Napier, Everett (C), Lloyd-Smith, Blanchard, Larkin, Goldie, Hopcroft, Tsunoda, O’Brien, Bartrip
Substitutes: Yanez, Erhabor, Enge, Sharpe, Howat, Weerden, Nolan, Swaby

items.summaryEn: Watch the best of the action as we beat the Eagles in a London derby
bodyEn: We secured our second win of the U18 Premier League South season with a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace on Saturday afternoon.
Having opened our UEFA Youth League campaign with a 2-1 win over Napoli, we continued our positive form into domestic action with a hard-earned success against the Eagles.
Emerson Nwaneri opened the scoring 12 minutes before half-time, before a rocket from Callan Hamill doubled our lead late in the game.

items.author: Connor Booth

items.titleEn: Read Renée's Crystal Palace programme notes
items.summaryEn: Read our head coach's thoughts ahead of the Barclays Women's Super League game at home to Crystal Palace
bodyEn: Before every home game, Renée Slegers gives her thoughts around the team and our upcoming game in her manager's notes published in the matchday programme.

Ahead of our first Barclays Women's Super League match of the season at home to Crystal Palace, the head coach knows there's more to come but was happy with the grit and determination we showed to get over the line at Brighton last Sunday.

Hello and a very warm welcome to Emirates Stadium for the first time this season as we take on Crystal Palace in the Barclays Women’s Super League. I hope you had a fantastic summer and you’re ready for WSL football to be back. It was very important that our players got that time off so they could come back and hit the ground running. We’ve got a huge season ahead of us and we can’t wait to get started at home.

I’m really looking forward to the atmosphere we create together here. I love every moment of this job. I love training and all the days spent preparing at the training ground, but matchdays in north London, sharing everything with our supporters – those are the best days.

We love it here. It’s a big pitch, with big spaces that we want to use. We are expecting Crystal Palace to try to limit our opportunities and break in fast moments, so that’s what we all have to be really aware of. I’m really curious how they’re going to approach this match as a new arrival in the league. It’s new to them to come and play at the Emirates, so we have to be prepared too.

It was a really positive start to the season against Brighton. We got the win, we got the clean sheet and we know what a difficult side they are to play against. I was very pleased to see Lisa perform so well. She’s an incredible talent, but she’s also very humble and hardworking. She had a good pre-season and earned her spot. It’s the first game of the season. It’s Brighton away. That’s not an easy moment to step in and make your debut, but she did that so well. I’m really happy for her.

That being said, there’s still a lot more to come from us. We played a lot of really good football last weekend, but how can we bring that more consistently? How do we maintain our level over 90 minutes? That’s what we want to achieve this season. Throughout pre-season we spoke a lot about how to find those ways to win, whatever happens, and we got a tough game over the line. That’s what I’m really positive about.

Seven out of eight new signings were able to come in day one of pre-season, which has been really good for our connection. Even after just a month or so together, we look like one group. Even Élisa, who came in much later in the window, looks really good in training and she’s adapting so quickly. Everyone has done great work to make that happen: Everyone’s worked so hard on and off the pitch to build these connections: staff, new players, but also existing players. There’s still a next level to reach, but we’ve all invested so much. It’s so good.

As a team, we’ve spent time really considering how we can take the next step this year. I think it starts with really looking at the people in front of us. That’s step one. We have to balance team considerations in training with individual strengths and needs. How can we support? How do we connect? How do we play to everyone’s strengths? That’s why I was positive about our opening game. The mentality and resilience in the group required to get those wins over the line, even on a difficult day in January when the pitch is imperfect and it’s raining and it’s windy… that’s built now.

Whatever the circumstance, whatever the match, we always bring us to the game. We’ll continue to work on our ruthlessness, so when there are moments to kill the game and there are moments for us to score or stop the opposition, we’ll do it as a team.
The last piece of the puzzle is you. So come with us. We want to do this together. Let’s bring each other on the journey, let’s be there for each other and let’s create something special.
As our supporters, you always bring your dedication and energy and support. We want to do the same for you. So let’s take this next step together. COYG!
Read more about the game, as well as a host of other fantastic content, by buying the Arsenal v Crystal Palace programme either around the stadium or online.
items.author: Arsenal Media

items.titleEn: Saka savours big win after punishing week
items.summaryEn: Our winger was all smiles after 'really big win'
bodyEn: Bukayo Saka could not hide his joy after playing his part in an intense, hard-fought 2-0 win away to Sunderland on Saturday night.
The game pivoted on decisive moments that went our way, and our winger said it was typical of this team for players to come up with big contributions when it mattered most.
“Yeah, 100 per cent,” he said afterwards. “It’s been since the start of the season.

"This is a really, really big win. I enjoyed it a lot - it was tough, but a big moment with David, big moment with Bruno that really changed the game and helped us win. The goal was amazing. The way it went in, I enjoyed it, the celebrations, everything. It was a massive moment, a great moment for him, and he deserves it - he’s a top guy.

“Big contributions - not just from the starting players, but the players coming off the bench. And Bruno showed that today, and all the others that came on as well. We’re going to keep going as a squad and that’s going to give us a lot of strength for the season.”

This trip up north came just 72 hours after we’d beaten Napoli 1-0 in Italy to start our Champions League campaign, and ended a week that had begun with a comeback win over Chelsea at Emirates Stadium.
Given the gruelling schedule, Bukayo believes the win is even more impressive.

He said: “It’s been a massive week for us, there has been a lot of travelling, people don’t understand behind the scenes how it’s been, but I’m really happy with how we’ve managed this and to get three wins, three tough, tough games - it’s amazing for us, so credit to the team, the staff, all of us. We need to keep going - it doesn’t stop.”

Bukayo himself slotted home the second. His penalty deep into injury-time to seal the win was his third goal of the season, and 84th overall for the club, drawing him level with another Arsenal legend who wore the No. 7 shirt with such distinction, Robert Pires.
“I enjoy hearing those milestones,” he grinned, “so I’m happy! I was pleased to get that goal at the end, I’m very happy!”
items.author: Josh James

items.titleEn: Mikel Arteta says penalty given to Sunderland ‘unacceptable at this level’
items.summaryEn: Arsenal manager angry: ‘This can never be a penalty’‘It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing’Mikel Arteta’s delight at Arsenal’s latest win was tempered by his fury with the referee John Brooks as the champions triumphed 2-0 at Sunderland on Saturday night.Before Bruno Guimarães gave Arsenal the lead in a tight match that Régis Le Bris’s team were arguably unlucky to lose, David Raya made a brilliant save to deny Enzo Le Fée from the penalty spot. bodyEn: Mikel Arteta’s delight at Arsenal’s latest win was tempered by his fury with the referee John Brooks as the champions triumphed 2-0 at Sunderland on Saturday night.

Before Bruno Guimarães gave Arsenal the lead in a tight match that Régis Le Bris’s team were arguably unlucky to lose, David Raya made a brilliant save to deny Enzo Le Fée from the penalty spot. Arteta, however, did not believe that Ezri Konsa had hauled Dan Ballard to the ground, instead blaming the Sunderland man for pulling down his opponent.

“We had to overcome a really tough opponent in a difficult place,” said Arsenal’s manager. “Sunderland can suffocate you and they decided to be really physical and very direct and we also had to overcome a situation that, in my opinion was unacceptable at this level.

“I’m very worried and sad because this can never be a penalty. It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing. We have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the win and our momentum. I’m really sad. It should never have happened.”

Arteta, who was booked in the first half for persistently stepping out of his technical area, hailed Guimarães’s goal as “beautiful” after watching Bukayo Saka scored a second goal from the penalty spot in stoppage time, when Sunderland’s Reinildo was sent off for a second bookable offence.

Le Bris was left with mixed feelings. “I’m proud and disappointed, these are the two words that are in my mind at the minute,” said Sunderland’s manager. “I’m proud because I think we showed that we are really close to achieving something big against one of the best teams in Europe right now. After the first half we were a bit reserved with the ball I think, but our second half was excellent.
“We got the momentum, created chances and it was a big save from Raya from the penalty. I think it was very good goalkeeping rather than a poor penalty. Raya was absolutely impressive today.
“We stayed in the game and we created other chances but we didn’t score and that was the difference today.

“We had intensity and togetherness and we were brave as well at times with the ball. We were flexible tactically because this Arsenal team creates chances. Today we found a solution to stop them and we created chances as well so it shows that we are getting better. It’s not enough yet but we are close.”
items.author: Louise Taylor at the Stadium of Light

items.titleEn: Arteta – “It doesn’t get much better than that!”
items.summaryEn: The boss praises the impact of 'finisher' Bruno Guimaraes
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta praised the attitude and performance of his team after we signed off a tough week with our sixth straight win.
After beating Chelsea last weekend, and seeing off Napoli in Italy just three days ago, we turned in a superb performance to defeat Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.

Two moments of magic, from Bruno Guimaraes and David Raya, ultimately decided the game in the space of two second-half minutes. First Raya made a superb penalty save low down from Enzo Le Fee, then just 121 seconds later, substitute Bruno cracked home a superb strike to break the deadlock.
From then on we stood up to the physical challenge to see out another clean sheet, and a sixth straight win to start the season.

“It’s a huge win, a huge week as well,” the boss said afterwards. “Winning against Chelsea, winning in Napoli and now here - a really tough place to come, what a beautiful atmosphere and a really well-organised, really well-gelled team, that makes life really difficult for you.”

Mikel said there were plenty of aspects of our performance that pleased him, but said he was especially happy with how we approached the game. “We were on the front foot right from the beginning,” he said. “it’s a game that shifts momentum a lot - the moment you make a little mistake, a little foul or a throw-in, the momentum shifts. Then you need to cope with the rollercoaster of that, emotionally it’s a game that requires a lot from the players. We were on top, then an element of suffering - obviously then the decision of the penalty comes in that can change completely the course of the game.

“David makes an unbelievable save afterwards, and then the magic moments that Bruno did as a finisher, it doesn’t get much better than that - an unbelievable goal, and unbelievable assist to put Bukayo through, and we earn the right to win the points.”

It means we maintain our 100 per cent start, and improve on last season’s 2-2 draw away to Sunderland. The manager said it’s another sign of improvement in the squad: “That’s what we want, but again, big credit to Sunderland as well, the way they play, the way they compete, how intelligent they are through certain phases of play.

“Also our supporters were again unbelievable. I’m so glad that the players went there and connected with them (after the game) because they were loud, they win with us, and hopefully they can enjoy the three points home.”
items.author: Josh James

items.titleEn: Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal: Premier League – as it happened
items.summaryEn: Bruno Guimarães, Bukayo Saka and David Raya all had a hand in maintaining Arsenal’s 100% record against SunderlandSunderland parade new striker Juan Angulo, signed from Independiente del Valle last week, before kick-off at the Stadium of Light. That one had passed me by – and I’ve spent all summer writing down hundreds of transfers for this …JD emails in …Here is my early prediction for very competitive EPL season. Teams will struggle to reach 70 points. The team getting 75 will surely be champions. Whether Arsenal get to ninety plus or they just about scrap to 70-75 remains to be seen. Continue reading...
bodyEn: That’s all from me. Louise Taylor has filed her match report from the Stadium of Light …
Arsenal go top of the Premier League before the Manchester derby tomorrow. Sunderland stay in the bottom half …

That’ll feel particularly sweet for Bruno Guimaraes, who scored such a wonderful opener on his return to the north east. The former Newcastle midfielder was booed throughout after his introduction at the break. Mikel Arteta’s decision to add a bit of poise to his midfield at half-time paid off.

Well, that was a battle. Sunderland were excellent, Arsenal resilient in their own way. Two key moments of quality decided it – the Raya penalty save and the Guimaraes goal that followed. Saka’s spot-kick at the end adds a bit of gloss to the scoreline.
The champions win again! Four out of four to start the season.
Saka goes bottom right and Roefs gets a hand to it but can only push it into the side-netting. All over.

Arsenal go up the end with Saka, who is being tugged into the area by Reinildo. As Saka goes to shoot, there’s enough contact to send him to the floor and John Brooks points to the spot. It’s a second yellow and a red for Reinildo. Saka will take to seal the points …
90+5 min: Roefs launches a free-kick forward. Ballard gets his head on another long ball forward but Brobbey can’t latch on to it before it reaches Raya.
90+4 min: Mukiele stops Merino on the edge of the Sunderland box. Brobbey gets his team up the pitch and throws himself at a Fofana cross but can’t get the right connection.
90+3 min: Arsenal win a throw in the corner but Havertz gives away a foul and goes into the book. Mukiele gives him a shove for good measure.
90+1 min: Six added minutes are announced after things have calmed down.
90 min: There’s handbags on the touchline as Guimaraes rolls around after a challenge – then rolls back on to the pitch. Isidor is the most aggrieved. Gabriel and Mukiele go on the book.

89 min: Saka escapes a booking for a trip on Danso. Sunderland send the big lads forward for Xhaka’s free-kick. Sunderland win a throw down the right – Mukiele launches it this time. Gabriel ends up on the deck and it’s a free-kick.
87 min: Xhaka is in charge of midfield now. Arsenal have a rare foray forward and Eze miscues a cross that lands behind the goal. Sunderland come again.

85 min: Big chance for Sunderland! Xhaka delivers a devilish cross into the middle and it bounces just in front of Raya, who flings his glove at it. The ball springs high and the goalkeeper gets there again, winning a free-kick in the melee. Merino replaces Odegaard.
84 min: Great effort from Mukiele! The ball bounces loose in the area and the defender’s scissor kick flies on to the roof of the net.
82 min: Arsenal changes – Eze and Zubimendi replace Rice and Tzolis. Feels risky taking Rice off now, but the man needs all the rest he can get. Zubimendi concedes a corner …

81 min: Gabriel makes himself even more unpopular by falling theatrically backwards when Brobbey gives him a shove in the chest. The striker goes into the book as Gabriel grimaces in ‘pain’ on the floor.
80 min: Sunderland are still creating openings and look dangerous. Fofana is causing Timber a few problems down the left wing. Arsenal are happy to sit and defend.
78 min: Timber has the ball in the net! He heads in an Odegaard free-kick but the assistant’s flag goes up straight away. Correct decision.
77 min: A Fofana cut-back causes utter carnage in the Arsenal box. Mukiele goes down under a challenge, then Isidor tries a backheel. Isidor and Fofana then go down and VAR says it’s all OK.
76 min: Attacking change for Sunderland. Fofana replaces Meunier down the right.

75 min: Big chances for Arsenal! Tzolis wins the ball and Odegaard feeds Saka on the right of the area. The winger’s shot isn’t great and it’s easy for Roefs to bat away. Saka’s corner is headed back into the six-yard box by Havertz at the back post and Ballard somehow heads it away from under the crossbar. Guimaraes then sends a shot wide.
73 min: Isidor looks of disdain back at Ballard, who launched a ball long in his direction that bounces out for a throw. Calafiori takes too long over it and the throw is reversed.
70 min: Change for Sunderland – Isidor on, Angulo off. They’re going two up top, with Le Fee on the left.

68 min: Big chance for Arsenal! Saka finds Havertz in the area but the striker opts to cut the ball back instead of shooting. Ballard cuts it out with plenty of Arsenal players waiting. Xhaka is booked for a rash challenge on Guimaraes.
66 min: Arsenal win a free-kick near the centre circle when Saka goes down over an outstretched leg. Ballard is booked, possibly for dissent. Raya takes it short.
64 min: Rice fouls Brobbey just into the Arsenal half. Xhaka drifts it towards Ballard, Meunier takes a swing and there’s a VAR check for handball. Nope.

62 min: It’s non-stop this. Brobbey robs Tzolis on halfway and suddenly Arsenal are outnumbered. The striker delays a little too long and Tzolis wins it back, punching the air at doing so. Guimaraes is still being booed, maybe louder now.

60 min: Totally against the run of play, that. Just after Raya’s penalty save, Arsenal made hard work of defending another Danso long throw before going up the other end. Guimaraes, the £75m summer signing from Newcastle, took the ball on the edge of the box, set himself and curled it into the top corner to Roefs’ left.
Guimares silences the Sunderland boo boys with a wonderful curling effort into the top corner from the edge of the box!
Oh wow! It’s a gut-punch for Sunderland!
Le Fee goes to the bottom right and Raya reaches it, brilliantly tipping the ball on to the post!
There’s some pushing and shoving around the penalty spot, just as there was in the box during the throw-in. It all simmers down, leaving Le Fee to place the ball on the spot …
54 min: Angulo wins another throw-in. Danso tosses it into the box again and Konsa wrestles Ballard to the floor. John Brooks points to the spot!

52 min: Gabriel claims he’s been elbowed by Ballard at the long throw but, really, it’s not much and not intentional anyway. The Brazilian has to leave the field for one minute, as per the new rules, after the game is stopped. He spends it speaking to Arteta in the technical area.
50 min: Boos greet every Guimaraes touch of the ball. Sunderland keep Arsenal boxed in the corner as Sadiki wins another throw for Danso to launch into the area. Raya claims this one easily.

48 min: Almost an Arsenal calamity on the long throw as Raya and Gabriel go for the same ball! It drops to Ballard, who takes a swing at it and sees his shot blocked. Brobbey asks more questions of Konsa on a following break before Sadiki fires over.
46 min: The second half starts as Rice steals in before Brobbey can collect the ball on the edge of the Arsenal box and boots it clear. Danso will wind up a long throw for Sunderland …
Two Arsenal changes: Guimaraes and Timber on, Lewis-Skelly and the injured White off. Former Newcastle player Guimaraes gets a healthy booing as he enters the pitch.

“A return to form for Saka would be the icing on the cake,” says former Arsenal defender Martin Keown on TNT Sports at half-time. I’m not sure there is a cake to ice just yet. Tzolis has looked a more creative presence for Arsenal out wide, with Saka on the end of a couple of chances. You get the feeling that, in this form, Odegaard will come up with something eventually.
Arsenal have had a couple of decent chances but Sunderland have been more than competitive. Brian Brobbey has been pretty immense holding the ball up against Gabriel and Ezri Konsa.
The half ends with Xhaka intervening with his heel as Havertz tries to head in Saka’s header across goal. The referee blows for half-time before Arsenal can take the corner.
45 min: There’s one added minute. Timber is stripped and ready because White has tweaked something. Arteta will wait for the break.

44 min: Havertz stretches to get his head to the Sunderland corner and it’s behind for another one. Raya gets a fist to the next one before Le Fee drags a low shot wide of the near post. Sunderland have had a good few minutes.

42 min: Angulo robs White of the ball in the Arsenal half and sets off towards the box. After a stepover and a ball roll, the winger throws himself to the floor as White steps across him. Meunier’s shot is blocked out for a corner.

40 min: The loudest cheer of the night comes as Arteta is booked for leaving his technical area too far and too often. He reacts with a tickbox gesture towards the retreating fourth official, who had clearly snitched.
38 min: Konsa and Raya appeal for fouls as Xhaka swings the ball in. One of them is given and it’s a free-kick to Arsenal in their own box.

36 min: Calafiori gives the referee an earful after Brobbey bumps him over at the resulting corner. VAR have a look for a moment or two but dismiss the claims. Sunderland then come forward as Mukiele drives into space. His low shot is blocked by Gabriel’s outstretched legs. Sunderland win a free-kick in a crossing position on the right …
items.author: Billy Munday

items.titleEn: Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick save
items.summaryEn: As the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.Two minutes after David Raya had rather majestically saved Le Fée’s second-half penalty, Guimarães delighted his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs from the edge of the area. Continue reading...
bodyEn: As the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.

Two minutes after David Raya had rather majestically saved Le Fée’s second-half penalty, Guimarães delighted his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs from the edge of the area.

Mikel Arteta’s champions were en route to another win in a campaign that has now produced six victories in six games in all competitions, including the Community Shield. No one, though, should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty; this was most definitely the toughest test this term for Arsenal.

If Sunderland can keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris and his players should have real cause for optimism – even if they could have done without Reinildo’s late sending-off for felling Saka when conceding that penalty and collecting a second yellow card.

His penalty miss aside, chapeaux off to Le Fee, who has deservedly made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from longlist to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.

Arsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.

There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery. Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20-yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.

Mikel Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the outstanding Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.

Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing or winning his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever-combative centre-forward, Brian Brobbey. If a packed Stadium of Light enjoyed that little subplot, the roof was nearly lifted off by the roar of approval that greeted Reinildo’s full-blooded early challenge on Martin Ødegaard.

One constant was Arteta’s excursions outside his technical area and eventually the referee, John Brooks, responded by jogging over to the touchline and waving a yellow card in the Arsenal manager’s face. While that booking was hardly unmerited, it seemed a shame that Brooks turned a blind eye to some persistent shirt-pulling from both sides at corners.

With the match even at the interval, Arteta replaced Myles Lewis-Skelly and the hobbling Ben White with Guimarães and Jurriën Timber. The Brazilian’s past as Newcastle’s captain ensured Guimarães’s every touch was booed, while Sunderland started the new half strongly, with Brobbey continuing to bully Konsa.

A penalty area encounter with Ballard at a throw proved no more welcome and when Konsa grappled the defender to the ground, Brooks – much to Arteta’s chagrin – had no hesitation in pointing to the spot.

Le Fée attempted to squeeze his kick just inside an upright but Raya, excellent throughout, guessed correctly and tipped the ball quite brilliantly on to the woodwork. Talk about a sliding-doors moment. Two minutes later and very much against the run of play, Arsenal broke from another Sunderland throw and Guimarães did the rest.
With no option but to take risks, Le Bris switched to 4-4-2 and also introduced Malick Fofana, newly signed from Lyon, and he quickly created chaos in Arsenal’s box.

Although it took Roefs, who saved superbly from Saka, and Ballard, responsible for a vital header off the line, to keep Le Bris’s side in the game, while Timber had a headed “goal” disallowed for offside, Arteta had reason to look slightly nervous as Mukiele volleyed Le Fée’s corner over the bar.
By now Xhaka, booked for sliding into Guimarães, was enjoying himself in midfield and from one of his corners Mukiele again went close.
A comeback beckoned but Saka had different ideas as Arsenal issued a reminder that they will not surrender their title lightly.
items.author: Louise Taylor at the Stadium of Light

items.summaryEn: Goals from Bruno Guimaraes and Bukayo Saka give us a hard-fought win
bodyEn: We maintained our 100 per cent start to the season with a win that all hinged on two second-half minutes.
After a robust, but goalless first half, the game exploded into life ten minutes after the restart.
First David Raya superbly saved an Enzo Le Fee penalty low down to his left, and two minutes later we broke the deadlock in stunning fashion.
Bruno Guimaraes fired home his first Gunners goal into the postage stamp of the top corner from well outside the area to silence the home crowd.
Bukayo Saka added a penalty late in stoppage time to seal the win in a feisty, physical encounter at the Stadium of Light, and make it 12 points from 12 at the start of the season.
HAVERTZ GOES CLOSE

There were no clearcut chances for either side in the opening 15 minutes, until Declan Rice found Saka inside the area with a lofted pass over the backline. Saka timed his run perfectly, but couldn’t get enough of a connection and Robin Roefs easily saved.
At the other end, Dan Ballard nearly got on the end of a Granit Xhaka curling free-kick that travelled through the six-yard box and away to safety.
Gabriel was given space to advance outside the Sunderland area until he decided to try his luck, but his low shot was dragged wide.

We finally got in behind the stubborn Sunderland defence on the half hour. Martin Odegaard drifted into space on the left, got to the byline and pulled the ball back for Kai Havertz. His first time left footed effort went over from six yards out though.

The German’s next chance two minutes later was much more difficult, but he made the keeper work this time. Chesting down Odgaard’s cross, back to goal, he spun and hooked a shot goalwards, which Roefs did well to tip over the bar.
The hosts retained a threat going forward though. Brian Brobbey was occupying our centre backs well with his strength and hold up play, while the set piece delivery also tested Raya.
The half ended with a timely clearance from Xhaka under his own bar, with Havertz lurking with the intent of converting Saka’s cushioned header across.
RAYA TO THE RESCUE
The manager made a double change at half-time, bringing on Bruno and Jurrien Timber for Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ben White. It was Timber’s first action since the Champions League final.

The hosts took the initiative at the start of the half. A long Kevin Danso throw nearly caused confusion between Raya and Gabriel as they went for the same ball, before Ezri Konsa had to have his timing spot on with his sliding tackle to deny Brobbey on the break.
Danso’s next long throw resulted in a penalty award to Sunderland. The referee was adamant that Konsa hauled down Ballard at the near post and pointed to the spot.
Le Fee stepped up, only for Raya to dive superbly down to his left, and push the effort onto the post and away.
BRUNO'S BELTER

Just 121 seconds later, we were ahead. Rice had a bit of space outside the area, but instead of winding up for the shot he shifted it along to Bruno. The Brazilian picked his spot with a stunner. Inside the top corner off the crossbar to register his first Gunners goal.
The former Newcastle man’s half-time introduction had predictably been met with boos from the home fans – this strike was the perfect response.

Saka had the chance to double our lead with 15 minutes remaining, but Roefs was equal to his low shot. The chance was created by a super piece of control on the run from Christos Tzolis, to find Odegaard. The skipper advanced with the ball before releasing Saka on the right.
SAKA SEALS IT
Bruno shot wide from inside the area before Sunderland threatened again on the break. The ball fell to Nordi Mukiele in the six-yard box, but back to goal he tried a backheel, which didn’t come off.

As time began to run out, Timber had the ball in the net when he headed in a lovely Odegaard free-kick, but he’d drifted just offside. At the other end Raya made another great save to deny Mukiele at close range, after the Frenchman slid in at the far post to meet a deep cross.

The game remained fiercely competitive, with both sides operating at full throttle, and was only settled when Saka won, and then scored, a penalty deep into injury time. He was released by a fine pass from Bruno, and burst into the area, where he was felled by Reinildo Mandava. the Sunderland man received a second yellow card and his marching orders, just before Saka stroked home his third goal of the season, to seal our sixth consecutive win to start the season.
WHAT'S NEXT

Our third of fourth consecutive away games is against Ipswich Town on Tuesday night in the Carabao Cup third round. We then head to Brighton in the Premier League next Saturday before a double international break.
items.author: Josh James

items.titleEn: Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning
items.summaryEn: English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighterPremier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neu
bodyEn: Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.
items.author: Jacob Steinberg

items.titleEn: ‘Delay the meals’: Mikel Arteta reveals latest maverick Arsenal methods
items.summaryEn: Manager wants players to cope with things going wrongOther tactics include making dressing room even hotterMikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.Arsenal’s flight to Italy on Tuesday for their Champions League opener against Napoli was delayed for more than five hours, with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time. Continue reading...
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.

Arsenal’s flight to Italy on Tuesday for their Champions League opener against Napoli was delayed for more than five hours, with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time.
The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner.

Arteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previously employed pickpockets during pre-season training camps and preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker.

The Arsenal manager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else.
“Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.

“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘OK, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but ­certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”

Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or ­surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”

Arsenal travel to Sunderland on Saturday night looking to extend their 100% start to the new campaign after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last year. Leandro Trossard scored Arsenal’s second goal before Brian Brobbey’s late equaliser and Arteta contrasted the Belgium forward’s reaction to leaving in the summer with that of Gabriel Jesus, whohas complained that he was kept in the dark over his future before being sold to Barcelona. “No one told me nothing,” said the Brazilian, who was made to train separately from the rest of Arsenal’s squad before moving to Barcelona. Trossard, meanwhile, was at the Emirates for last week’s win over Chelsea having joined Beskitas in July.

“Very surprised, to be fair, especially because with Gabriel I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” said Arteta. “And the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don’t know. It’s OK. Sometimes I understand when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don’t expect. Those things are reactive. Somebody has to be the bad cop; if I have to be, I have to be.

“What is important is normally what happens three months later, six months later. When Trossard comes in, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relation you have with all the players that they left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that’s the same case.”
items.author: Ed Aarons

items.titleEn: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend

bodyEn: With 10 top-flight goal contributions between them across three games already this season, the Chelsea trio of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer are the early pace-setters for the Premier League’s most prolific, fluid and high-octane attacking unit. But on the occasion of his 100th Premier League appearance, a scruffier and more ungainly unit will be hoping to steal their thunder, as high-flying Hull try to register a top-flight win against Chelsea for the very first time. Yet to score this season but with a couple of near misses to his name, what Oli McBurnie has thus far lacked in goal contributions he has more than made up for with selfless graft and off-the-ball grunt work, making a total mockery of Steve Clarke’s decision not to include him in Scotland’s World Cup squad. The Hull striker ought to prove a real handful for a decidedly porous home defence, and a goal would be a fitting way to mark a century of Premier League appearances. Chelsea have not won any of their past four league matches against promoted opposition and, given Hull’s blistering start to the season, victory on Saturday seems anything but a foregone conclusion. Barry Glendenning
Chelsea v Hull, Saturday 3pm (all times BST)

This might be an opportune moment for Álvaro Arbeloa to meet Andoni Iraola, though perhaps not his Liverpool team. With three defeats and seven goals conceded from his first three Premier League games as Fulham head coach, questions are already being asked over the former Liverpool defender’s ambitious approach. Just as they were when Iraola failed to win any of his first nine league games in charge of Bournemouth. Trust yourself and the process, might be the Liverpool head coach’s advice if asked. Fulham have been creative under Arbeloa but are easily exposed defensively. Liverpool, starting to click in attack under their new head coach, have the assets to exploit Fulham’s weaknesses and subject Arbeloa to an uncomfortable Anfield return. Iraola’s wide options could be reduced, however, with Bradley Barcola suffering cramp on Wednesday – his first start since France’s World Cup semi-final loss – and Cody Gakpo nursing a minor injury. Andy Hunter
Liverpool v Fulham, Saturday 3pm

Cheick Doucouré has had a rotten run of luck with injuries. Just when the Mali midfielder looked as if he was ready to make a first Crystal Palace appearance since January 2025 in Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Middlesbrough, he was taken ill. Pierre Sage revealed last week that Doucouré looked as if he had “given him one million dollars” when he was informed he would be part of the matchday squad at Fulham, where Palace got off the mark with a 3-2 victory. Sage has confirmed that the 26-year-old, who has been sidelined with two serious knee injuries but was once a transfer target for Liverpool, could be involved against Ipswich at Selhurst Park on Saturday. Whenever he does return it is sure to be a heartwarming moment. Ed Aarons
Crystal Palace v Ipswich, Saturday 3pm

The midfield battle between Brentford and Bournemouth will be crucial on Saturday, with Vitaly Janelt and Mamadou Sangaré setting the tempo for Keith Andrews’ physical side. Brentford top the Premier League for aerial duels won (22.3 per 90 mins), interceptions (11.3 per 90), and fouls committed (16.3 per 90). “They defend well as a team, their high pressing is good,” said Bournemouth’s Marco Rose, who is hoping to guide his side to a first Premier League victory of the season. “Their transition, they have fast players. They have quality everywhere on the pitch, and every situation.” Rose’s answer for Brentford’s aggressiveness should be Alex Scott, who leads his team for interceptions and has drawn nine fouls so far this campaign – the fourth-highest tally in the league. Late drama could also be the deciding factor at the Vitality Stadium. Despite leading in all three of their opening league fixtures, Bournemouth have picked up just two points and four of their five goals conceded have arrived from the 84th minute onwards. History favours their opponents too, as the Cherries have failed to win any of their eight top-flight meetings with the Bees. Yara El-Shaboury
Bournemouth v Brentford, Saturday 3pm

A summer of change at Aston Villa inevitably prompted plenty of noise but most of their new signings were long-standing targets, none more so than Nicolas Jackson. Unai Emery kickstarted Jackson’s career at Villarreal and, after reuniting at Villa, the Senegal striker scored his first goal at Club Brugge on Tuesday after his initial £47.5m move. Jackson has replaced Ollie Watkins, who proved a reliable source of goals across six straight top-flight seasons, and the early evidence has been encouraging. “I had a couple of fights with him when he was at Chelsea so when he first came in I thought: ‘What’s he going to be like?’ but he’s a brilliant guy,” said the Villa captain, John McGinn. “There’s a lot of expectation with the transfer fee but he’s going to be a huge player for us.” Ben Fisher
Aston Villa v Nottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm

Only the most pessimistic home fans at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium will be gripped by anything resembling the kind of dread, anxiety and outright terror that accompanied Everton’s visit on the final day of last season, but the return of David Moyes’ side so early in the current campaign will still make for nervous viewing. With no goals and just one point on the board after three league games, fan faith in Roberto De Zerbi – and the hundreds of millions of pounds lavished upon new signings – has created a prevailing presumption that Tottenham will soon start firing on at least some, if not all, cylinders. In Everton, Spurs welcome a team whose record in this corner of north London is worse than any other top-flight side’s. Should they fail to beat a team who have taken just seven points from the past 51 available to them away at Tottenham, the sounds of early but outright mutiny are likely to be audible from the stands. BG
Tottenham v Everton, Saturday 5.30pm

Old acquaintance will be renewed at the Stadium of Light on Saturday evening. While Sunderland’s captain and midfield anchor, Granit Xhaka, needs no introduction to his former north London public, the home centre-half Dan Ballard is a former Arsenal youth captain who joined the Gunners’ academy at the age of eight. Then there is Bruno Guimarães. Newcastle’s former captain can expect a hot reception as his new side aim to extend their season-opening run of five straight wins (including the Community Shield). “Arsenal are flying, they’re one of the best teams in Europe,” says Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager. “It will be challenging but I’m very excited to experience this situation again.” Thanks to goals from Ballard and Brian Brobbey, Le Bris choreographed a 2-2 Premier League draw against Mikel Arteta’s side on Wearside last November. “When you face a strong opponent you can become a bit shy but the most important thing is to be ourselves,” says Le Bris. “Arsenal are so adaptive they will find solutions, so we must be flexible.” Louise Taylor
Sunderland v Arsenal, Saturday 8pm

One of three teams, along with Aston Villa and Tottenham, yet to score a top-flight goal this season, Coventry were extremely unfortunate not to break their duck at Manchester City last weekend. Their having narrowly avoided handing Frank Lampard’s side an early opener, it took a string of excellent saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma to ensure City took three points at the death. “They played really well against Manchester City and created a lot of chances,” said Fabian Hürzeler, who takes his Brighton team to the CBS Arena on Sunday afternoon. Having been scathing in his criticism of his own side’s lack of energy and intensity in their woeful first-half performance against Leeds, the German will be aware that a similarly lethargic performance from his team is unlikely to go unpunished. Particularly away from home against a promoted team that may be firing blanks, but visibly grew in confidence with each passing minute of their defeat by one of the league’s best teams. BG
Coventry v Brighton, Sunday 2pm

Manchester derby No 199 features a fascinating showdown between two young managers operating in the sport’s rarefied air: Michael Carrick, 45, who seeks to guide Manchester United to an 82nd victory in the fixture, and Enzo Maresca, 46, who aims for Manchester City’s 63rd. As the great Pep Guardiola’s successor, the visiting Italian can be delighted at his team’s perfect record from their four games under him since the Community Shield defeat. Carrick, though, should be disappointed at the return from an opening three matches as United’s permanent manager: a defeat at Hull and draw at Everton, with the 5-2 home win over Ipswich sandwiched between. United fans will protest beforehand about the club’s approach to eradicating ticket touting, and the occasion should be particularly spicy and vibrant. Jamie Jackson
Manchester United v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm

Two teams unbeaten in the Premier League this season, two German managers in the dugouts and a Monday night goalkeeping beauty contest at Elland Road. While Daniel Farke welcomes his compatriot Matthias Jaissle to West Yorkshire for the first time, James Trafford – the £40m England keeper Newcastle tried to sign on three separate occasions – will be in goal for Leeds. The visitors eventually turned their attentions to the £26m Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who arrived on Tyneside from Braga in July. So far at least, Jaissle is delighted by the 24-year-old’s performances. “Lukas is an amazing signing,” said Jaissle. “Coming to the Premier League and dealing with the pressure is not easy and, as a keeper, that pressure is something else. I like Lukas a lot. He’s so calm but so mature as well. There’s not even a hint of nervousness. He gives the whole team confidence. That helps a lot.” LT
Leeds v Newcastle, Monday 8pm

bodyEn: During Covid, when sport was back but behind closed doors, I hosted a number of strange online shows to fill the void of real life. The highlight was chatting to Darren Gough about a lifesize bronze rhinoceros for 45 minutes to 15 small boxes on a Zoom call. I don’t recall who it was for and where the rhinoceros came from – but it might be in his garden.

I ended up doing virtual pre-match corporate Zoom calls for Heineken before Europa League games. It was the wifi version of Club Wembley: a Q&A happening on stage between a generic host and some random ex-pro while you’re trying to chat to your mate and eat an unidentified square of meat with some dauphinoise potatoes.

I’d be in my little square talking to Luis García in his little square about the ghost goal while an assorted group of faces and living rooms or kitchen tables would stare at you, perhaps interested, perhaps not. Did they even want to be there? Were we on mute while someone from marketing was filling a spare box on my laptop watching Death In Paradise on the TV behind me?

Certainly it was hard to create an amazing vibe with Mark van Bommel while his internet connection crashed and a little note on a Google doc appeared telling me to fill for 25 minutes with my favourite memories of the Europa League. Did these disembodied heads in front of me want the deep dive they got on Tony Parks’ heroics in 1984? How many of them knew about Gary Mabbutt playing centre mid and marking Enzo Scifo out of the game?

One of the guests was Dimitar Berbatov. You’d log on half an hour before the show and say hello, try to build some kind of electric rapport with a man in Bulgaria (I think) presumably looking to get in and get out and get back on with whatever social distancing life in Sofia had to offer.

He may have not had Akabusi levels of energy, and his economy of language was not unlike his playing style – why use a hundred words when one will do? But he was into it and did the job perfectly. I absolutely loved Berbatov as a player. Watching him pluck a goalkick out of the sky was more beautiful than watching a lot of other players banging one in from 25 yards. There’s a YouTube video called Dimitar Berbatov – the most underrated first touch ever? It begins with him standing like a lamp-post on the halfway line at Craven Cottage and stopping a crossfield ball stone dead like it’s an anvil.

Back to the Zoom call: I welcome Dimitar, he says hello, I explain my admiration for him, and then say to him that he made football look easy. Did he find it easy? “Yes” he replied. Totally matter of fact. Not trying to impress – just explaining that football was easy.

And for someone like Berbatov, it is a different level to “good touch for a big man”. This is the ultimate type of grace on a football pitch. And perhaps it is reserved for tall, skilful players. I’ve probably used the word languid already but I can’t think of any other use of the word – reserved for players who are almost balletic.

Is it insane to say it’s more aesthetically pleasing than seeing a Messi or a Maradona waltz through a defence? It almost feels as if a low centre of gravity gives you an unfair advantage when it comes to technical skill. No flailing arms and legs to get in the way of you being naturally brilliant.

My biased brain instantly goes to Glenn Hoddle walking through the Oxford United defence with one sway, sitting the keeper down with a movement of the leg. It’s all saying: “This is easier for me than it is for you.”

Which brings us to Kai Havertz – and that dummy against Chelsea. The more and more football becomes that David Mitchell sketch, the more surprised I am that there are still moments in a game that lead to some involuntary noise from deep within.

The ball from Christos Tzolis is definitely for him. Havertz points in front to where he wants the ball. If it’s played there he can probably get a shot away first time. But when it comes, controlling the ball would have been a sensible choice. Back to goal. He could have turned and shot, or just kept the ball. There are lots of good players to pass it to.

Even the way he lifts his left leg at the last second to let the ball run through to Martin Ødegaard is delightful. It’s easy to forget the pace of the game at this level. And when you’re watching on TV where it’s much easier to see the pass you also forget these guys don’t have that view.

Someone somewhere will have done a report on Havertz’s scanning abilities. He doesn’t appear to look behind to check where Ødegaard is. But awareness is hard to calculate. He just knows. And he does it all in a split second, not even. How wonderful that you can do so much without even touching the ball.

A lot of people do quite well out of repeatedly asking whether Arsenal need a centre-forward, so I don’t want to do them out of work. And Havertz isn’t perfect – he isn’t Robbie Fowler in the box. But he has scored in two Champions League finals. He did win the league last season. A lot of beautiful graceful players tend to be beautiful and graceful without delivering on the biggest occasions. Havertz does both. And when he gets it right, it looks easy to him. Imagine finding it easy.
items.author: Max Rushden
